utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Prosecutor versus Zejnil Delalic, Zdravko Mucic, Hazim Delic, and Esad Landzo. Case number IT-96-21-A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Appearances, please, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honour. I'm Upawansa Yapa, appearing for the Prosecution. With me is Mr. Roeland Bos. Mr. George Huber is the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Obviously, nobody on behalf of Mr. Delalic. For Mucic, Mr. Morrison. For Delic, yes, Mr. Karabdic. And for Landzo, Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Perhaps because we haven't been here for awhile I should check whether each of the accused can hear the proceedings in a language which they understand. Mr. Mucic, are you able to hear the proceedings in a language which you understand? Thank you. Mr. Delic? Thank you. And Mr. Landzo? THE APPELLANT LANDZO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, each of you have given us notice that you wish to attend. I assume the Prosecution is here simply to answer things rather than to raise something.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well, then. Well, Mr. Morrison, you're here for Mr. Mucic. You're the next one on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: If it please Your Honour. I am acutely aware that I suspect we are all here to some extent to wait to see what other people are saying and to respond to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, that's very interesting. That's a long way to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't for me but it was for some people, I appreciate that. There are, however, two issues which arise in the case of Mr. Mucic. The first is this: Obviously, and I accept that the judgement will be delivered as soon as practicable, but Zdravko Mucic wishes to make it plain that given his current sentence under Dutch law, he's been advised by Mr. McFadden that as matters would stand on his existing sentence, he would be due to be released in early November. I don't know what the position is going to be as to the date of the delivery of judgement. It may be that the judgement would be delivered prior to that actual release date; it may be that it will not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Morrison, you have told us on a number of occasions that you have judicial duties yourself to perform from time to time, and you know that there's no way I can tell you when the judgement will be given. It is well under way and will be given as soon as it can possibly be given. I don't want to give you any hope that it will be given on any particular day or by any particular time. It's simply a matter of ensuring that five Judges can agree upon its terms, which is a bit more difficult than I should think you have to worry about yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have enough trouble agreeing with myself on occasions. I'm fully cognisant of the problems of multiplying that by five. The second matter is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: In relation to his sentence, it was seven years, wasn't it? And you're assuming that he's going to be kept in the Netherlands, which is an assumption I don't think you're entitled to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, not an assumption that I've made but a matter of practical advice that has been tendered to Mr. Mucic by Mr. McFadden at the prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, that if he was being kept by the Dutch authorities, then that's so. But he's being kept by the United Nations' authorities at the moment in an area within the Netherlands, and he's not kept pursuant to the Netherlands' release provisions. But there are others that have got two-thirds, and I can see that it must run out -- seven years from, when was it, the 18th of March, 1996, so it must be sometime in November, two-thirds. Of course, he may be sent to Spain, and Spain has three-quarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I can't say I'd object myself to having a hearing in Spain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no, not a hearing in Spain, but he may have to serve his sentence in Spain. I shouldn't be light-hearted about it. It's obviously a very important thing. I can only say that it's unfortunate that this appeal took so long to get under way because of the parties' manoeuvrings over a period of, I think, nearly 18 months before we got under way. However, that's something that's gone by the by, and we will keep in mind your client's rather precarious position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: That's all I ask, Your Honour. The second point is one which I fully appreciate is not necessarily within the bailiwick of your normal powers or responsibilities, but Mr. Mucic is anxious that it be raised, and that's this: He has, during his time in custody, had very few visits. He has a son and a daughter in Austria who have visited him on two or three occasions over his period of custody, but no one else. There is, in fact, a couple who are not related to him, Mrs. Bloemkoelk-Turk and Mr. Colakovic, who have made repeated requests through Tom Kuzmanovic to be allowed to have a visit, and it's not met with favourable response from the administration. The reality of the position is that if those people would be allowed to visit, it can do no harm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are they resident here in the Netherlands?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: They are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. As you have foreseen, it has really nothing to do with the Tribunal or the Appeals Chamber. It's a matter which if you don't get satisfaction from the superintendent, from memory, you go through the Registrar to the President. And may I suggest that that's what should be done. I don't know what the regulations are about how closely people have to be related before they're allowed to visit. It seems to me that that's a matter, though, that could well be ventilated -- I don't think there's an appeal, but I think there's some sort of administrative procedure that you have to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour will understand that it's a matter of importance for the client to have the matter raised in court, and of course the suggestion which Your Honour has made is one that can be pursued, and I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Karabdic, what do you want to raise on behalf of your client?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please be advised to turn on the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The issue which I was about to raise with you, in fact, has been answered now, which is that my client has been in detention for a long period of time, since the sentence has been passed, the judgement has been passed, about two years ago, and he is living in uncertainty. He would like to know when this final judgement is going to come down. He is aware that the Appeals Chamber is working and that it will do its best to issue the judgement as soon as it is practicable. However, he is trying to deal with this uncertainty, but I believe now we have heard an answer coming from you and we'll have to wait. He also has problems with visits, but we believe that we can solve these problems with the management of the Detention Unit. He is not able to get all the visits that he wants, but I believe that we can solve these problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed. Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Your Honour, Mr. Landzo has one problem which he has tried to resolve with the administration of the Detention Unit without success, and which I have also made some representations on his behalf, and that is this: He suffers very badly from asthma. Your Honour, he has had during his time in detention quite a number of visits with the medical advisor, the doctor, to the Detention Unit, and also with representatives of the Red Cross, and he's made a number of requests through administrative channels that the Detention Unit take some steps to provide a segregated area for those who do not smoke. Apparently, Your Honour, the presence of cigarette smoke is very prevalent in the Detention Unit and his condition is worsening because of that. Your Honour, I've had the opportunity to talk to Mr. McFadden myself on that subject, and the issue seems to be this: Obviously, there are some instances in which Mr. McFadden has to segregate certain detainees from others; some of these, of course, by personal animosities and some by ethnic divisions. And he tells me that quite a high percentage of the inmates do smoke. Your Honour, my position on behalf of Mr. Landzo is simply this: Given what one knows these days about the effects of secondhand smoke, it is unreasonable for Mr. Landzo to be detained in an environment where he cannot escape from that. Several different floors are available at the Detention Unit, and it is my submission that it would be a reasonably simple matter to provide a floor, or part of a floor, for those prisoners who do not smoke, or particularly those who cannot tolerate cigarette smoke. Your Honour, given the length of time Mr. Landzo has been there, and of course we don't know how much longer he may be there, this is a matter which is, perhaps, deserving of the Court's attention. I would ask Your Honour to consider asking the Registry to have some dialogue with Mr. McFadden about creating this kind of environment for Mr. Landzo. Your Honour, it is an important medical concern; he's been advised that this is causing damage to his health.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: This is a matter which was raised, I remember, at the first of the Status Conferences under the amended Rule --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: -- and I said at the time to your lead counsel that it's a matter that if you don't get satisfaction from Mr. McFadden, you have to take it up through the Registry to the President. If there's one thing that any court must understand is that they do not have the expertise to run a gaol. It has to be done by experts. And I think you've probably referred to the real problems that do arise. I have had a little experience from being part of an inquiry into a gaol system once, and the problems are manifold. They're not as easy as even you put them. And I certainly am not in any position to say anything except to say you should take it up through the Registry or the Registrar with the President, and it may be that there can be something done. One thing that I have noticed since I've come to live in Europe is that the prevalence of smoking here is very much higher than anywhere else I've ever come across in my life, but that's general in the community; and to a non-smoker, I agree, it's not pleasant. But I can't say anything, I can't do anything, I can't give any direction, I can't give any advice. Mr. McFadden, I hope, has discussed it, but you may be able to persuade the President, perhaps, that something more can be looked at. But I can't really put the Appeals Chamber into the fight, if I may put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, of course, and I wouldn't ask Your Honour to make any positive indication beyond, perhaps, indicating on the record that it would be an appropriate matter for the Registry to discuss with Mr. McFadden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I really cannot buy into what I've described, perhaps wrongly in an international tribunal, but as a domestic issue. It really has nothing to do with us. And other than to advise you, or your client through you, that he has an avenue of review, I suppose is the best way of putting it, through the President, I can't really buy into it and put the weight of my authority into any part of this equation. I understand the problem, I sympathise with your client, but to tell the superintendent of the gaol, who has, I think, still only three floors, although I think they may have another area now, that he must segregate it so that there should be a non-smoker's area is just not part of my expertise. But it's now on the record, and you can probably use the transcript as part of your appeal to the President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There's nothing more I can say, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are other matters, but those are other matters which we can take up directly with Mr. McFadden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Yapa, is there anything you want to say about any of the matters that have been raised?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I do not think there are any matters on which we have a say, and we have no submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We're very grateful to you all for coming such a long way. I'm sorry that you don't get any particular comfort out of what's happened, but I think you may have foreseen that that must be the result. A Status Conference is not really for these issues. I will adjourn.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
